Buying a home on the Gulf Coast

From your first budget to the keys in your hand, here's how buying works on the Mississippi Gulf Coast, with the local steps people tend to learn about too late.

I've been investing in real estate for 15 years, and the biggest surprise for most buyers here isn't the price of the house. It's the insurance. I'll help you get real flood and wind quotes before you're locked in, so the monthly payment you plan for is the one you actually get.

Bill Temple, Realtor

01

Step 1: Set your budget and get preapproved

Know what you can comfortably pay each month, not just the loan amount.

Talk with a mortgage lender before you start touring. A preapproval letter shows sellers you're ready, and it tells you what price range to search.

When you work out a monthly payment, include more than the loan. Add property taxes, homeowners insurance, flood insurance if the home needs it, and any HOA dues. On the Coast, insurance can change the monthly cost a lot from one house to the next.

On the Coast

First-time buyer? Ask your lender about down payment help through Mississippi Home Corporation, the state's housing finance agency. Programs and rules change, so your lender can tell you what's available and whether you qualify.

02

Step 2: Price insurance early

Get flood and wind quotes on homes you like before you make an offer.

Find the flood zone for any address on FEMA's Flood Map Service Center. Zones that start with A or V are high-risk areas. If the home is in one and your loan is federally backed, your lender will require flood insurance. Homes outside those zones can still flood, and flood coverage there usually costs less.

Ask an insurance agent for quotes on the actual address. A standard homeowners policy doesn't cover flooding from rising water, so flood is a separate policy, through the National Flood Insurance Program or a private company. Wind and hail may come with the homeowners policy, or as a separate policy from the state wind pool. Ask what the hurricane or named-storm deductible is. It's often a percentage of the home's insured value, which can be thousands of dollars.

On the Coast

Features that help a home stand up to wind, such as a FORTIFIED roof certificate, roof straps, a newer roof or impact-rated windows, can lower insurance costs. Ask the seller for any certificates or reports they have.

03

Step 3: Choose your agent

Know who represents you, and put it in writing.

In Mississippi, an agent gives you a short form called Working With a Real Estate Broker early on. It explains whether the agent represents you, the seller or both.

Under current rules for agents who use the MLS, you'll sign a written buyer agreement before you tour homes with an agent. It spells out what the agent does for you and how they're paid. Agent pay is not set by law and can be negotiated. Read it, ask questions, and only sign what you're comfortable with.

04

Step 4: Find the right town and home

Compare towns, commutes and elevation, not just the house.

The Mississippi coastline runs about 60 miles, from Waveland and Bay St. Louis in the west to Ocean Springs and Pascagoula in the east. Each town has its own prices, taxes and character. Think about your commute, how close you want to be to the water, and what you need in a yard or garage.

For each home, check the flood zone and ask whether there's an elevation certificate. Look at the roof's age, the drainage around the house, and how high the home sits compared with the street.

05

Step 5: Make an offer

Price, terms and timelines all matter, and so does the seller's disclosure.

Your offer covers more than price: earnest money, how you're paying, the closing date, and how many days you'll have for inspections and insurance quotes. Your agent can show you what similar homes sold for, and the market update shows how fast homes are selling right now.

Ask for the seller's Property Condition Disclosure Statement and read every page. It asks whether the home is in a FEMA flood hazard zone, whether it has ever flooded from rising water, whether flood insurance is required and what the premium is, and about any water or storm damage. Under Mississippi law, if you get the disclosure after your offer is accepted, you have 3 days after it's handed to you (or 5 days after it's mailed) to end the contract by written notice.

The disclosure shares what the seller knows. It is not a substitute for your own inspections.

Gulf Coast market update

06

Step 6: Inspect the home

Use your inspection days well. They go fast.

Hire a licensed home inspector to look at the roof, structure, plumbing, electrical, heating and cooling. Most buyers here also get a termite (wood-destroying insect) inspection, and many loans require one. Ask whether the seller has a termite bond that can transfer to you.

For older homes, consider a sewer line camera inspection. Homes built before 1978 come with a lead-based paint disclosure, and you have the right to a lead paint inspection. A survey shows the property lines and any easements.

Use these same days to firm up your insurance quotes. If an inspection or a quote turns up a problem, you can ask the seller for repairs, a credit or a lower price, within the terms of your contract.

On the Coast

Ask your inspector about the roof's age and how it's attached, signs of past water in the walls or crawl space, and how water drains away from the house. These are the things insurers on the Coast ask about too.

07

Step 7: Finish the loan, appraisal and insurance

Line up coverage early so it doesn't hold up closing.

Your lender orders an appraisal to confirm the home's value, and needs proof of homeowners insurance (and flood insurance, if required) before closing.

New flood policies through the National Flood Insurance Program usually have a 30-day waiting period, but the wait generally doesn't apply when the coverage is required for a new loan. Ask whether the seller's current flood policy can be transferred to you, since that can sometimes keep the current pricing.

08

Step 8: Close and get your keys

Walk through the home, sign, and stay alert for wire fraud.

On the Mississippi Gulf Coast, a real estate attorney or title company usually handles the closing, checks the title and records your deed. Your lender's closing disclosure, sent at least three business days before closing, shows your final costs. Compare it with your loan estimate.

Do a final walk-through to make sure the home is in the condition you agreed to and any promised repairs are done.

Before you wire any money, call your closing office at a phone number you already know is real to confirm the instructions. Scammers send fake wiring emails that look real. Closing offices don't change wiring instructions by email.

09

Step 9: After you move in

File for homestead, and get ready for storm season.

If the home is your main residence, file for Mississippi's homestead exemption to lower your property taxes. You must own and live in the home on January 1, and you apply at the county Tax Assessor's office between January 1 and April 1. Bring your closing papers.

Keep your insurance policies, closing papers and any elevation or roof certificates somewhere safe, with copies online. Before hurricane season starts on June 1, make a photo or video inventory of your home and belongings.
